timeline.draft_answer: The catastrophic double glacier collapse in Tibet in 2016 was investigated by an international team of researchers from ETH Zurich (the Earth Observation and Remote Sensing Group and the Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology - VAW), the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research (SLF), and the GAPHAZ commission (Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains). They analyzed numerous satellite images and used the SLF-developed RAMMS simulation software to reproduce the avalanche and create precise elevation profiles of the glacier prior to the collapse. After the first ice avalanche on 17 July, they detected a line on the neighboring glacier nearly identical to the rupture line of the first collapse, indicating an imminent second collapse. They modeled the risk, produced a hazard map, and warned Chinese scientists and local Tibetan authorities through GAPHAZ; the second collapse occurred only a few hours later on 22 September 2016. The findings suggest that geological and topographical factors, meteorological conditions, and most likely recent climate changes all played a role in why two neighboring glaciers collapsed in such a similar way and close in time. The event also marked a milestone in the development of early warning systems, as satellite images could be analyzed with only a few hours' delay.
